I made this guide because I could not find one that completely satisfies YouTube's recommended specification, and there is no guide for 5.1 audio on YouTube. This method is easy on your editor software and produces the best quality video possible for YouTube. If you want a shortcut, use any other capture guide. This is hard mode for people who want perfection.

Bookmark this page. This is what YouTube wants you to upload. You don't have to match this spec, but any deviation from it means you are compromising some aspect of your video when you don't have to. I am going to share my workflow since it's pretty simple and you can get higher quality than the spec, meaning you are going 10/10 for your viewers. This method will also scale to larger resolutions better than other methods because the file system I/O is your bottleneck, not CPU or GPU.

Every part of this guide represents some form of compromise. I have catered my methods to make the compromises in a way that suits playing a game while capturing. I use Sony Movie Studio 13 as my editor and transcoder for this guide, which isn't free. You can get the same results with HitFilm for free, but it doesn't do 5.1 audio output. (I bought the codec pack too)

Required Software

  • MSI Afterburner this also appears to wok with Bandicam, but that costs money and I haven't tried it.

  • Audacity

  • Razer Surround You need this for the surround audio capture, otherwise skip it. Surround gaming headphones that have their own windows audio device should work also, but I haven't tried it.

  • Sony Movie Studio. Put it on your Steam wishlist as I got mine for $29 and it's the only way to do 5.1 without Vegas Pro or Premiere. You can also use HitFilm if you don't care about surround.

  • MediaInfo You use this to verify your work.

  • MPC-HC This allows you to play your raw capture and switch audio tracks while the video plays. VLC works just as well.

If you want to stream to Twitch while you capture, use OBS (not multiplatform), use nvenc, disable instant replay, and set it up so it streams only. This will cause your recorded gameplay to not have your camera in it. You may want this for editing a YouTube video without a camera. There may be a way to include your camera in recording. This guide will not cover it.

MSI Afterburner is the current superior choice for game capture because it allows you to capture with an intraframe codec and it records 8 channel audio in a separate track from your mic. This is important for editing because it will be much less taxing on your computer when you are previewing your video before rendering, you get a perfect copy of every frame of gameplay, and you don't have to clap sync your mic.

Install MSI Afterburner and configure your video capture like this with the following exceptions:

  • Set your Multithreaded operation to 2 less than your CPU cores, as Windows sees it.

  • Audio source #1 should be your desktop audio device. If you install and set up Razer Surround and use it for your source, you will get 8 channels of audio in your first track.

  • Your mic device should be Audio #2 unless you want to capture Teamspeak as separate audio as well. In this case, set your TS audio output to the same device your Razer surround output and choose that device for Audio #2. There is another way to do this if you are doing stereo gameplay audio. Ask in the comments if you care. If you are not recording your mic here, use Audacity to record your mic and clap sync it to your video.

  • Enable MJPG encoder is for Premiere users, it otherwise doesn't matter

Start playing a game and capture your gameplay using the hotkey. This will be the result of your game capture file when you check with MediaInfo. Notice the very high bitrate and separate audio tracks, also that it is 60fps exactly. This video file is as close to lossless as is practical for editing purposes and the separate mic track is always preferred. Congratulations, you now have the best raw materials available for creating your video. If you have ridiculous amounts of space available in a raid, you can set the video to YV12 for a little better quality at twice the size.

We now need to organize the audio tracks with Audacity because Movie Studio doesn't know how to deal with the audio and won't import the tracks without some help. This only takes a few minutes to do, once you are familiar with the steps. Open your capture video with Audacity. You should get this screen asking which stream you want. Select the top one and you will get 8 separate wav tracks like this.

The order from top to bottom is: front left, front right, center, lfe, rear left, rear right, side left, side right. You can export these now using File>Export Multi, but I like to make the front, rear, and side tracks into stereo so it imports into the editor with fewer steps. Center and lfe need to remain mono tracks.

To make the front stereo track: pan the left track to the left, the right track to the right, select both tracks using Shift+click, and use Tracks>Mix and Render. Repeat this for the rear and side pairs of tracks. Don't do any adjustments to the audio, like compression, since you might mess up the surround balance. You can adjust the volume in the editor.

Once you are done with the gameplay audio, repeat the process with the bottom stream and this will be your mic audio. Do all the effect editing you want and export the stream using File>Export Audio. I prefer to use 32 bit wav because it is fast.

If you combined your tracks you should have 6 audio files now. Three stereo wavs for front, side, and rear; three mono wavs for center, lfe, and mic. Open Movie Studio, import your video and audio tracks, and drag them to the timeline. If you did everything correctly, all your tracks will line up exactly and will look like this. Now you can edit your video as long as you cut all the tracks at the same time and keep everything lined up. Your mic should be set as a center channel. The side channels should be panned to the center, leave the adjustment alone. Some games like Warframe don't have side channel audio, you can ignore those tracks in that case.

I won't cover the actual editing or effects here, that's up to you. Once you are ready to export, select Sony AVC/MVC in advanced export options and modify an Internet 1920x1080-30p template to look like this and this. Make sure to save your template so you can quickly select it for future videos.

If you did everything correctly, MediaInfo will look like this for the final rendered video. When compared to the YouTube spec it's a perfect match. You don't have to go to this much trouble, but this method ticks all the boxes and is the highest quality method I know of. Hope this helps you bring your best to your viewers. Feel free to ask any questions.
